extracted.intended_audience: current or prospective mathematics department chairs and academic administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluative standards for running a mathematics department: communication with dean/faculty, budgeting, raises, tenure and promotion cases, hiring, and when/how to step down. Focused on duties and best practices for chairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the Dean to the Department and vice versa
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chair's two chief jobs are (i) to explain the Dean to the Department and (ii) to explain the Department to the Dean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that the Dean will often be less emotional about administrative matters while faculty may get exercised about teaching loads, salaries, research records, etc. You will be blamed for unsatisfactory circumstances and may be seen as colluding with administration; manage expectations and mediate between the two sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Run the department openly and give everyone a voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Run your Department in as open a fashion as possible. Make extra efforts to be sure that everyone feels he/she has a voice in all important decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create many committees, appoint Deputies/Vice-Chairs/Associate Chairs to spread power and blame, hold frequent faculty meetings. These structures let people participate and reduce perceptions of unilateral action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain informal information pipelines (teas and accessibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hold frequent informal gatherings (e.g., teas) and attend them to allow faculty to interact with you informally and 'sound you out on key issues.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular informal contact keeps information flowing, helps you gauge the 'air' in the department, and reduces misunderstandings. Top departments often have daily teas; adopt analogous low-cost practices where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be an active Chair who initiates improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: A good Chair has ideas and will start initiatives and make things happen—even if some faculty are intransigent and uncooperative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be a rubber-stamp. If you have a supportive Dean, they will back initiatives. But beware: if the Dean perceives you as a rabble-rouser you may lose support; balance initiative with political judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage perceptions to avoid being deposed
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep departmental unrest below an 'excessive' threshold in the Dean's view to prevent the Department from petitioning the Dean to replace you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If many faculty are repeatedly taking grievances to the Dean, this signals a leadership problem. Use openness, committees, and communication to defuse situations. If a groundswell to depose you arises, the Dean may call meetings and solicit new nominees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize when to cease being Chair
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sensitive to when it is time for you to cease being Chair: if you have stopped being effective, cannot garner cooperation, research or personal life is suffering, or a strong successor exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chat with colleagues and family; be realistic and mature about stepping down rather than remaining ineffective or burning out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and manage the departmental budget
rubrics_metrics.description: Your Department will have a budget comprising faculty and staff salaries, supplies, travel, visitors, colloquia, computers, and miscellaneous funds; your job is to come to terms with it and make the most of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn that departmental budgeting differs from household budgeting. Identify fungible parts, cultivate skills to pry extra resources from the Dean, and plan within fiscal constraints. Expect large-department budgets to be multi-million-dollar enterprises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate donor and special funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek out alumni and donor funds for distinguished speakers, visitors, travel, and other enrichment activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such funds can substantially enhance departmental life and give flexibility for last-minute visitors or temporary positions; most departments will not have generous unencumbered funds, so pursue donors where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set pragmatic limits for travel/colloquium/supplies
rubrics_metrics.description: When doling out discretionary funds (e.g., travel, colloquium, supplies), operate within limits—often modest (example: $500 per request).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate with Graduate Studies or other offices for graduate travel support; be transparent about limits and prioritize to maximize departmental benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate faculty raises by merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not give everyone the same dollar amount or the same percentage increase for raises; raises should reflect merit and contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make and be able to defend hard decisions about raises. Discuss evaluations with the Dean, and when possible have candid annual discussions with faculty explaining why the raise level is recommended and what could improve it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use individual consultation to set expectations for raises
rubrics_metrics.description: Privately meet with faculty each year to review contributions (teaching evaluations, publications, service) and explain recommended raises and ways to earn more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you plan to tie raises to increased duties (e.g., more teaching) or productivity (more publications), ensure the Dean supports this approach and that you can follow through.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a salary committee as an objective buffer
rubrics_metrics.description: Form a small committee to evaluate Good Works Forms/annual reports and recommend raises (e.g., categorize into Meritorious/Good/Fair).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A committee creates distance from personal complaints and provides a documented, more objective rationale for allocations; committee members should recuse from their own raises for that year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give something to everyone to preserve morale
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule of thumb, give everyone at least something (avoid 0% raises) to maintain departmental 'Gemütlichkeit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even a small raise (e.g., 1%) for those who are not causing trouble helps overall morale, though this may slightly reduce funds available for top performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegate and manage staff raises appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: For staff raises, consult the head secretary for recommendations; the Chair typically handles the head secretary's raise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empower the head administrative staff person, who often knows staff contributions best; involve them in recommending fair increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemble a complete tenure dossier via a committee
rubrics_metrics.description: Form a tenure committee to build the case: solicit outside letters, collect teaching information, and report on departmental/university service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The committee prepares a recommendation (tenure or not) and presents the dossier to the Chair and Department. Be thorough and follow institutional procedures and etiquette for outside letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chair's veto and quality control of tenure cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chair may have (rarely used) veto power to stop an inadequate tenure case before it proceeds to higher levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise veto if dossier is clearly flawed (insufficient papers, poor journals, uneven teaching, weak outside letters) to avoid embarrassing failures at the Dean's level; weigh this choice carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department discussion and voting on tenure cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Hold a departmental meeting where the tenure committee presents the case, a vigorous discussion occurs, and a vote (often secret ballot) is taken aiming for a strong majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain standards and seek consensus; close votes are problematic and may displease the Dean. Different departments have different voting rules and requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outside letter standards and etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: Outside letters should explicitly state whether the candidate deserves tenure, make binary comparisons with peers at a comparable level, and speak in detail about the scholarly work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be courteous to letter writers: explain local guidelines in the solicitation, thank them afterward, and (where appropriate) inform them of the outcome. Solicitors should avoid overburdening famous scholars with frequent requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare to present and defend the tenure case to Dean and committees
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chair typically presents the dossier to the Dean's Tenure & Promotion Committee and must be ready to answer pointed questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that the Dean's committee will scrutinize research quality; the Chair should craft a persuasive presentation and anticipate criticisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand successive review levels (Dean, Provost, Trustees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenure/promotion cases progress from Department to Dean (and Dean's committee) to Provost (broader view: teaching and citizenship) and finally to Chancellor/Board of Trustees who may occasionally intervene for non-academic reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect different emphases at each level and be prepared for rare political or ideological interventions by trustees; document and justify the case thoroughly at each stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chair's cover letter for tenure/promotion dossiers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chair's cover letter (about 3–8 pages) presents the case: assesses outside letters, evaluates teaching, and summarizes service; it should be incisive, compelling, and honest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address evident flaws forthrightly and highlight strengths. Keep the letter concise (not fewer than 3 pages, not more than ~8); show drafts to Executive Committee/trusted colleagues and revise carefully. Overlong diatribes (e.g., 18 pages) are counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mid-tenure (3-year) and annual junior-faculty reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a 3-year (mid-tenure) review with ~2 outside letters, careful teaching evaluation, and service review; annual reviews are lighter (no outside letters) with small committee reports and one-page summaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these reviews to give candid feedback; meet with the junior faculty member, ensure they understand shortcomings and steps to improve, and involve senior mentors when appropriate. Frequent check-ins help correct course early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about non-traditional scholarship for junior hires
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that Deans and committees at many institutions value traditional, peer-reviewed publications; non-traditional outputs (e.g., extensive web-based scholarship) may be viewed skeptically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise junior candidates to understand institutional norms and tailor publication and dissemination strategies accordingly; at established institutions, traditional peer-reviewed outlets carry more weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hiring: oversee candidate evaluation and departmental involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Department has a position, the Chair oversees bringing candidates: meetings, talks, interviews, and departmental interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hiring involves broad faculty participation and affects long-term departmental profile. The Chair should evaluate how a candidate contributes to research, teaching, and departmental development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess candidate needs and sell hires to administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine candidate needs (salary, startup funds, spousal hires, leaves) and make the case to the Dean/administration for necessary resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For senior or exceptional hires, build a persuasive case (e.g., show competing offers from top institutions) to secure competitive salaries/perks. Learn the vocabulary and tactics to 'sell' candidates to the Dean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design appropriate interview/visit requirements for job candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: Set the 'hoops' for visiting candidates (talks, dinners, possible teaching demonstrations like a calculus lecture) depending on the nature of the position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor the visit components to evaluate candidate fit for the department's needs; some institutions require public talks plus pedagogical demonstrations to assess teaching ability.
